utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning everyone. Do we have something before we continue? Why do we not have the witness? Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know why the witness isn't here, but I just want to introduce, if I may, Shubhangi Bhadada, who is from Delhi, India, and a graduate of the master's programme at the University of Oxford in law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness. Mr. Nicholls, I was wondering whether you were not minded to tender the interviews -- the part of interviews you dealt with with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, Your Honours, I think I would tender those portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How shall we identify the parts? Do you have any objection, Mr. Robinson, in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think it would be -- since the parts were read out to the witness that he commented on, I don't think there's any need under your practice to now retroactively go back and add them to the record. If there was something at the time that was covered, they should have been put to the witness or else -- I don't see any value in repeating what's already in the record by having the interview itself admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the interview themselves were read out in full. And further, in order to understand the context of the conversation referred to the witness, I think it's important to -- at least those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I would just at add that at the beginning and in some areas because of time I was summarising parts of a paragraph and to show that I was summarising it accurately, that part of the page it would be useful to have in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, I would recommend the parties to communicate each other what parts are to be tendered, and let's see what parts Mr. Karadzic may be also dealing with with the witness, and at the end of the session let's discuss the admission of the parts of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Later, if we have enough time, I will ask you to clarify a few things following from a difference in language and the semantics. But now I would like to ask you something about the things which the OTP suggested to you. It was suggested to you that more was known and I knew and that I was concealing something. Can you please tell us this: According to the knowledge you had, were there any unlawful killings in Srebrenica before the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I knew, what I looked into and did, there had been no unlawful killings up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I'm rushing. And it was also suggested during the cross-examination that I sent you with certain intentions to Srebrenica. Was it because I issued you such a task or was it on your own initiative that you went to Srebrenica in connection with any sort of unlawful killings or any other unlawful activities?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must expand this a bit. If you will allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you can just briefly reply and then we may expand.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here, I have told the Prosecution too, answering with a yes or no falsify my entire activity in Srebrenica. During the 15 days of the Srebrenica action, I physically stayed in Srebrenica on duty only for three hours and I had one telephone conversation with the deputy centre chief. That was all of my activity during 15 days. And then to make a complicated construction so as to fit everything in into a joint criminal enterprise, up until the moment when they got the documents that show that I never signed a single document with regard to Srebrenica, not just because I didn't know and knew what I was -- what was going to happen because I wasn't in the seat of the ministry at the time and I was only organising the Sarajevo front at the time and I was even a suspect for a while. So we should avoid this sort of false construct. With the three hours of my stay during the -- a fortnight and one telephone conversation, this is all of my activity in connection with Srebrenica, as I've told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to object as non-responsive, but I think he's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I will now try to simplify matters so you could answer with a yes or no. It was suggested to you that I sent you there. Did I send you in Srebrenica at all, and was it my or your or anyone else's initiative by which you sent members of MUP to commit murders in Srebrenica or do anything else unlawful?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did I -- I didn't send anyone. I didn't -- I wasn't, as you well know, involved in Srebrenica at any stage except for the establishing of the police station in Srebrenica. That was the only official duty that I received, that I was involved in, and that during my three-hour stay I inspected and made sure that the police station would be established. As for all other activities, I was not in charge of them nor did I want to be involved, not because I knew that something could happen but because I did not believe that this front was serious enough at the time and the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you first tell us, would it be usual for the minister and the deputy minister to be resubordinated to the army? And what did you mean when you said that you did not consider this front to be serious enough?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here, Mr. President, from the very first moment when I opposed to being engaged in Srebrenica, I was aware of the much wider activity on lifting the blockade of Sarajevo and I knew that Srebrenica was a bad tactical move, where we would become involved in something and get bogged down and that we shouldn't have done. But the decision was up to other people and not up to me, and that was the reason why, from the military point of view, I considered Srebrenica not to be such a threat as Sarajevo, not even close. It was quite clear to serious military experts, but when we look at all this from a different angle and consider the consequences of the events, then the Srebrenica front gains more weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was your question or the translation. Your question as translated reads like this: "... would it be usual for the minister and the deputy minister to be resubordinated to the army?" Is it the minister or the deputy minister that is to be resubordinated to the army? If you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Well, when Mr. Karadzic said "minister or deputy minister," he actually had in mind the same function within the ministry. It's not usual that they can be resubordinated to the army, only if one of them directly commands a unit which as a unit is resubordinated specifically that particular unit. But as an organ, as an institution, it's not usual, it's not even lawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber what you know from official documents and my activities, what was my position about the treatment of prisoners of war, including this case in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say in my answer that through my operative investigations, I can only tell you that in this way, through the focus of my operative investigation, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but briefly. So were you aware of my position? On the basis of documents and my activities, what was my position?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two periods in work with you: 1992 and 1995. During 1992, as one can see from the documents, I came, I saw that you directly -- then it was collection centres, camps which showed up that directly, through your documents, orders, pleas, you requested that all conventions be honoured and that everyone be treated adequately. And in 1992, through a memo of the government, we adopted that all the organs had to do that in that way. In the analysis of Srebrenica, you returned to 1996 and it was again you who requested and asked, in 1995 and 1996, that all conventions be honoured, that certain tasks be carried out with regard to civilians and everything else that cropped up at the front, and eventually in 1996 you requested an investigation. And when I saw this and I said in front of the OTP investigators, I uttered a sentence that if you were once again in a situation to launder them, the famous sentence, I didn't mean to launder the situation; but if you were again in a situation where the relevant organs, military prosecutor's offices, courts, security organs, were not doing their work properly, everyone who had to do this by default, by applying the law, so that the final results would be presented to you and that you were the one who requested them to take measures. And that was a problem of the entire situation. That was the greatest problem that occurred for us in the Srebrenica area, namely, that the organs who were supposed to do their work did not know how to do it and did not want to do it properly. I'm sorry that I left my position at the time so I couldn't complete this work as I did it in 1992 and 1993 and all other years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly have a look at P2995, please. It's a document which the MUP sent on, it forwarded it. P2995, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can read it out to you and others may check it on their screens because I can't see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha, here it is now. Please have a look at it. Then you don't have to read out aloud. Please have a look at item 4 and tell us how this relates or how it fits with your experience with the treatment of the prisoners of war, my position about this, and the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this item in the evidence. In 1992 it was formulated, this item 4, in which you ordered -- we cleared this up in 1992, how the civilians and POWs and persons who committed some criminal offences were to be treated. This is completely clear for anyone who wanted to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you that I tried, including my orders and the one dated the 1st of April, 1996, that I tried to cover up these events. Did you understand then or did you understand from this document that its intention was to cover something up?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I expand on this a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please be as brief as possible, but you may.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A problem here is this: What I have gone through and from what I have seen, there was this one position in Srebrenica where you had the security organ who was supposed to implement the conventions, participate directly and order to the effect to prevent the commission of crimes. Then there is an organ who was supposed to collect information and send them to you. It's the same organ. But there was this decadence, this blockade, this subordination of a higher organ in relation to the lower one in carrying out the tasks and lack of respect for higher instance and the supreme commander in the chain of information leading up to you. That happened to you. You were blocked by these organs, the military security organs. I established that clearly. I saw it clearly. I saw it clearly. When you came in the position, in order to be in a position in the month of April, to send this to all the addressees, the military investigation organs or police organs, you tell them to take measures, you tell them that you have information and that they should take measures against this war crime, things had to be quite the opposite. Those military organs were not doing their work properly with regard to the state and with regard to you personally. So this is my view. I don't think that at any moment you were laundering or covering up anything there. But you were in a position, just like in early 1992, where you had to request from organs to do something, to do some sort of work, which they were supposed to have done already because that was in accordance to the law. And here we have an even worse case where the organ who was supposed to do something like that was directly responsible for committing such acts. So I don't think that in any way whatsoever you were covering up anything, but you had opportunistic and incapable organs at that moment, and I think that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to that effect it was suggested that Mladic's diary --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P1490. The typewritten version, please, Serbian, page 44; English, page 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read these first two paragraphs and could you tell us what the reason was for me, on the 22nd of March, to be bringing up this topic again. Was it aimed at a cover-up or what was it aimed at, the first two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- I don't think he can comment on what President Karadzic's motivation and what was in mind was at the time that he said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly Mr. Karadzic could reformulate his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this meeting, this request of mine in relation to Mladic, what does it tell you? Is it counting on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's -- let's let him read the passage first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can read it out loud if you want.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A big show was put on for Albright. She expected they would find 1.200 Muslim corpses at Pilica, but they found some five corpses. "We met (Koljevic, Biljana ...) and concluded that it was best for a parity commission to be formed to really investigate all the deaths and killings around Srebrenica during the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does that fit into your knowledge, what you knew, about the treatment of crimes and covering up crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not fit into covering up crimes. In my view, the process of opening the Srebrenica problem lasted. A continuity can be seen here of the Srebrenica problem. It was supposed to be investigated and sanctioned at state level, so I see this as an unstoppable continuity, a continuity that was unstoppable. Now, whether it should have happened earlier, that's a different question. So I see it as -- I mean, we can see part of the process here already, opening up this problem, and your instruction comes on the basis of the continuity of the knowledge that you received. That is how I see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But by this time you knew the locations of crime site, didn't you, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the autumn of 1995, I carried out operative investigations and I would not focus on the locations. I did not deal with the locations in principle. In global terms after this investigation, I knew; but I was investigating other reasons at the time when I was minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with hindsight on your part, read this first sentence, to say that there were 1200 Muslim bodies in Pilica, it could not have been a big show at all. It's true. Do you have any say to such observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot in terms of such a formulation -- well, I tried to present my point of view. As for this kind of formulation and answer, I cannot say what it was that people specifically saw in Pilica at the time and what was in Pilica. At that time, I was not in the area. Now, in the meantime, whether it had remained as it had been, I cannot say anything about the time when I was not minister and when I was not physically present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's put it more directly. You, as the minister of MUP or deputy minister of MUP, you knew what happened in vague terms, and you said Mladic should have been arrested immediately. And then you say Mladic and Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Mladic didn't know what happened at all by this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. You see, this conversation here, conveying sentences from a diary, first of all, I have to tell you straight away, as far as Ratko Mladic's diary is concerned, I do not accept it. I do not recognise it. I think it is a construct. I do not think that these are writings of a normal person. There are quite a few elements of schizophrenia here and I can see that, and I talked about it to experts too. And as for these formulations, I mean, well, giving an answer, but everything that is here, that is bandied about here before this court concerning Ratko Mladic's diary, I think that any normal person would not want to comment on anything that is contained in this diary. Knowing what happened and comparing what this diary contains to what I know from before and the distortions and -- I really would not want to comment on anything stated in General Ratko Mladic's diary. My friends who are experts clearly established that there are certain elements of schizophrenia in the way in which events are viewed and registered in this diary. So I really wouldn't want to -- I mean, that's why it's not easy for me to say something about some of the things that he establishes in this diary because these constructs and these statements -- I mean, they're quite schizophrenic. The best thing would be for me to say what I have to say, but everything that is put in this diary -- I mean, it's -- it cannot be normally -- I mean, it has to be viewed in a different way, interpreted in a different way. That is my position in general terms, vis-à-vis all the facts contained in Ratko Mladic's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Well, if you believe this is a construct, then there would be no point on your part answering any question with respect to any passage there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think there are other things. I mean, after all, as far as this diary is concerned, on my part, regardless of whether there are some correct statements there, from my point of view there is no point in my responding to anything that is contained in Ratko Mladic's diary. My mind of a policeman and my mind in general cannot accept this diary of Ratko Mladic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on the subject, could you please look at paragraph 5, what that commission is supposed to be like. I'm going to read it out. "If they expand the campaign, then they would form a Joint Commission (one from civilian security, one from army security, and two from the United Nations) to investigate the killing of every individual." Does that look like an intention to cover something up and would this kind of commission be fair?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly a correct attitude in terms of the heterogenous composition. Certainly there could not have been a cover-up. This is serious work on establishing facts, I mean as regards the graves and the factual situation in terms of what happened in the area. So this is a normal, solid foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry. Is it -- translation -- who are "they" here, Mr. Kovac? "If they expand the campaign, then they would form a Joint Commission ..." Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't ask me. This is not my formulation, "they." I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, I've already said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you do not understand this paragraph, how can you answer the question put by Mr. Karadzic, whether it was a cover-up or not? How did you understand this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood this sentence and in response to a concrete question about the composition, the composition of the commission that is supposed to work on that. So it's quite clear, heterogenous commission, that's that. However, "they," for me the word "they" is a third party, the international factor, international institutions, there is no other way I can interpret this. I didn't really go into that. That's probably what they meant. I think they meant the international factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, during the cross-examination you were asked about this possibility that Bajagic, Deronjic and others could have informed me. Did you have any information to the effect that they had informed me about executions of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have such information that they informed you directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any written report that would contain this information about executions in Srebrenica that would have been sent to me?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: An attempt was made here to explain the wording of "he had to know." This past participle in the English language, could you explain that? Actually, could you explain this participle in different terms? Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we be more specific? Shall we upload the document if you're referring to a specific passage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the part that was shown by the distinguished Mr. Nicholls from the interview, 2003, I believe. In response to whether he knew, the answer was: He had to know or he must have known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's -- because we are dealing with, shall we upload 65 ter 25350, e-court page 43, where you said: "This is crystal clear because he," being Mr. Karadzic, "he had Bajagic who knew everything ..." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I could not have said he and Bajagic knew. No, no. I don't have the translation here. Please let me see this. I need to see it clearly. I could not have put Karadzic and Bajagic together, no, no, no. Give me the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do we have another translation referring to that situation? This is the only one? I didn't understand past participle, but let's deal with this passage first. Unfortunately, we do not have the Serbo-Croat transcription, but I take it we have audio-tape if necessary. And this transcript says that you said: "This is crystal clear because he had Bajagic 'who knew everything.' He had Deronjic, he received all the information that he needed from them ..." And this passage was dealt with in cross-examination by Mr. Nicholls, and you said: "I absolutely stand by that statement."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a different construction for all of this. I said clearly that people came who were in charge of informing him about Srebrenica, not that they informed him about crimes in Srebrenica. And when I stated that it was perfectly clear who the persons were who were in charge of informing Karadzic about Srebrenica, he put the names there, meaning Deronjic, I did not have the obligation to -- or I was not involved in the Srebrenica operation. It was perfectly clear that there were people who were in charge of informing Mr. Karadzic about Srebrenica. What kind of information they provided and how they provided this information, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, back to you, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- sorry, just you'd asked me earlier if there were any other passages that deal with this. There's a -- it's also dealt with on the top of page 52 of the same interview, 65 ter 25350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it covered by your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I didn't bring that one up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to read out your answer from line 22 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, another part that was covered in my cross-examination was at e-court at page 50 of this same interview, just to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we're going to call up that page too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But let us just read this answer of yours. [In English] "If I may say, I don't see any name of any VRS official. It would be logical for Tolimir or Beara," and some -- "TK also said, 'or Salapura or Mladic' or people at these positions to come Tomo Kovac in fact said, 'to be invited to come' and report to him, but they were not there, Tomo Kovac also said, 'they probably did not want to come, I don't know.'" [Interpretation] Did you know that they had come? What does this assumption of yours -- I mean, this assumption in terms of logic, where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean Tolimir, Beara, Mladic, and so on. On what do you base that assumption, that it would be logical for them to provide information?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logical in terms of their obligation on the basis of the law and their function and the establishment of military command and reporting from the front line. That is quite clear. That is the route according to the law in Republika Srpska, and that is the way these people who were supposed to inform the supreme commander about that were supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 80, you tried to say that this was not within your domain, that it was the domain of investigation and reporting. Whose domain was that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to clarify a bit. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 40 you were asked whether you had investigated and reported. You said that was the purview or the domain and then you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was meant. I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one word. Was the conduct of military structures in the purview of the police -- military police?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a theatre of war, in a combat zone, the treatment of prisoners of war is in the exclusive purview of the military security service, the military prosecutor's office, and their military judiciary. So the police force cannot take any action vis-à-vis the army or the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the meetings you had at the Presidency during those days, and you maintained that Srebrenica was not a topic, that the topics were mainly centred around Sarajevo. Can you tell me, regardless of the agenda, did anyone mention the execution of prisoners of war on the 13th of July, when we met one on one? Was there anything to report on the 13th of July when we met?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not report to you about Srebrenica at that time, and you know very well that I was focused at that time on the Sarajevo theatre of war. You know that I expressed my doubts even concerning the Sarajevo theatre and even told you that you did not realise how serious the situation was and how easily it could fall, taking down with it 150.000 people in that area. I knew that better because I came from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 14th you saw me alone again and then on the 15th in a larger group. I want to ask you about the meeting one on one on the 14th. Did we discuss Srebrenica and did you tell me about Kravica; and if not, why not? What significance did Kravica have for you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not report to you about that. I did not know about the weight of Kravica except for the killing of a policeman and the wounding of another policeman, and I had the report of Ljubisa Borovcanin that several prisoners were killed. That incident did not give me cause to report to you. On the other hand, I knew that the appropriate services and Ljubisa had the legal obligation to provide you with all these reports officially, covering all the steps that should have been taken and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did we discuss? What was the hottest topic, not only in Sarajevo but the entire Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a problem with the war in Krajina. Our lines were falling already at that time, and that was a topic in addition to Sarajevo, and also my demands for supply of material assets. And we had reports to discuss about the situation that reached you and the Assembly, although the situation on the ground was something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I show 1D71161 to the witness. 1D71161.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look. On the 14th of July, I issued this order to Municipal Assemblies -- it seems we don't have a translation yet. Which municipalities are concerned and what are the problems with refugees? What was ordered here to the Ministry of the Interior? Just give us your own account.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see clearly that at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there was a loss of territories and there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Since we do not have English translation, first establish with the witness what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to tell us what is this document? When was it issued? And to what municipalities is it addressed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was issued on the 14th of July, 1995. It was sent to Municipal Assemblies of Petrovac, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor, and to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to read it all. What does it concern?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing assistance to refugees, the population that had fled from municipalities that had fallen under enemy control, and it says that temporary accommodation should be provided to the refugees along with minimal living conditions. The Ministry of the Interior is to help the competent authorities in executing this order. And finally, regular reporting on this assignment is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document receives MFI number D3973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show 1D9767 in e-court, please. It seems we only have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it to you. 13th July: [In English] "Military/political situation in Serb Sarajevo satisfactory. "... at a meeting of the president of the Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic and president of the RS National Assembly Momcilo Krajisnik with representatives of Serb Sarajevo, the political and military situation was assessed as satisfactory. "After the meeting, the Serb Sarajevo mayor, Dr. Vojislav Maksimovic said the previous positions on the division of Sarajevo into Serb and Muslim parts is being supported. "'We can easily say that the situation on the fronts changed after the Muslim offensive on Serb Sarajevo was crushed and after the fall of Srebrenica ...'" [Interpretation] What did you discuss with me on that day, because you were with me one on one, whereas these other people came in a group? Did I need to see you before this meeting? How is this related to your discussion with me?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every minute of my discussion with you was the situation in Sarajevo, apart from the situation in the Krajina theatre. The first part of the offensive against Sarajevo was completed, another one was expected from the axis of Mount Treskavica and Mount Igman, which many people did not understand properly. And I insisted with you that all the structures should take this very seriously and focus on this. That was the gist of my discussion with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document and what I said to the mayor, is it a realistic view, a realistic description, or was it unwarrantedly optimistic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, optimism prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was recorded that this optimist version was intended for the -- for public use.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D9768. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it as Exhibit D3974.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9768.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a summarised report of the SRNA agency news for 13th July. What is the top story? Which theatre?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo theatre, obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph there is talk about this meeting, but I would like to read out to you the last paragraph. [In English] "Despite previous defeat, the Muslim leadership does not give up its offensive on Serb Sarajevo. Partial leader of the Bosnian Muslims, Alija Izetbegovic, visited Mount Cemer and, together with the Muslim Army commander, General Rasim Delic, persuaded his soldiers to again attempt to breach Serb lines in the north-west section of the Sarajevo front." [Interpretation] Is this a bit more realistic than those optimistic statements we'd seen before, and what does this say about the situation in the Sarajevo theatre?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This says clearly that all the Muslim forces were assigned to attack the Serb-held western Sarajevo and those positions there, and this was obvious to me from day one. It was clear to me that the beginning of the Sarajevo offensive was that first attack at the command of the VRS from the direction of Srebrenica; however, many people did not understand where the real problem lay so they focused more on trivial combat zones, trivial compared to the western theatre around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives number D3975, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In P2242, which is the agenda of my secretaries, the entry for that day, we see that on the 15th, General, you called on me, together with Mr. Krajisnik and Maksim Stanisic. Do you know which position Maksim Stanisic held at that time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was president of the Executive Board for the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Trivko Radic and Tomo Kovac. That should be page 92. Did you or any other participant of that meeting mention Srebrenica on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way, certainly not. We were talking about Sarajevo, the functioning of the local authorities, the police, the defence lines, and the provision of material assets and supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Trivko Radic's position was?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of the Vogosca municipality or president of the Executive Board or perhaps mayor of Vogosca. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of July, you visited again at noon, Maksim Stanic, Krajisnik, Tomo Kovac. Can you tell me, if you remember, what was the reason for this visit? Who was Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ninkovic was defence minister and Stanisic was the president of the city government. And the discussion at the meeting was about providing material and supplies to the Sarajevo theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We need to clarify a few things that remained unclear before. In cross-examination, Ibran Mustafic was mentioned. Did he survive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we see that item you referred to on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be on the next page, 93.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see the 18th. And in line that says "12.00," it's the fourth line for the 18th of July, both in the handwritten and the printed version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Mr. Kovac was not there -- oh, there, I see. Yes, thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's -- it was mentioned on page 24 of the cross-examination that the DB was collecting information and, inter alia, questioned Ibran Mustafic. Did Ibran Mustafic survive this interaction with the state security?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exactly -- I think he did, but I cannot -- I cannot say or I cannot exactly tell you at this moment what the state security was doing then and I wouldn't like to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's finish with the question of reporting. Did you ever intend to report to me that you remained in the position of the minister and at what moment would the conditions be created for you to report to me about this? What would it be so that it would be necessary for you to report to me?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in the initial stages of collecting information. I had clear assessments that those who committed the said acts in Srebrenica, specifically Beara and his team, the team from the state security, one whole chain of people, were very dangerous people at that moment, and that the preparation and collection of information for them and everything else that might follow would have to be a very serious and difficult action and that would certainly be carried out upon completion of the war operations. At the moment when I prepared -- when I had prepared everything, just like I used to do in the previous years, with all groups, you would then have it on your desk sent from me with a clear request that together with other institutions, as we had no powers -- that with other institutions, the judiciary and everyone else, such an action should be rounded off. So with the end of war and demobilisation of the army after Dayton, that is to say, what would certainly have followed -- it would certainly follow but -- please, I have this sound in my earphones, interpreters or someone, I don't know who it is. I'm having this scrambling noise in my earphones. It's certain that at the end of the war and after demilitarisation of the army, my activity would follow and a certain -- a serious briefing, but it's not a matter of briefing. When a relevant state organ briefs someone else, they have to have well-prepared evidence and also measures that are to be taken that are already prepared, rather than leave it to the president to prepare the measures because it's a burden for him. So it was a difficult situation and knowing what sort of people these were, what combination of people, because I had had a -- quite a long experience with Beara. He had -- he was a criminal mind. He had a problem at the Dubrovnik front earlier in the war. So considering all that, on the one hand you had the police, on the other you had military security administration, so much greater preparation was needed. It was impossible during the war because a civil war would have broken out. I waited for the war to end and, of course, I wanted to collect all the evidence to round it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First we have to see in lines 16 and 17 on page 26, you said specifically Beara and his team, the state security team. Did you mean the state security or the military security?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I meant the nomenclature from the military security, not the state security. Even if I said it, it was a slip of the tongue. Military security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure whether I understood your answer. The question was this: "Did you ever intend to report to me ... and at what moment would the condition be created for you to report to me about this?" What was your answer in short -- in brief terms? Did you ever intend to report to the president, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I hadn't, I wouldn't have said that. As soon as I would get close to the stage where I had more collected evidence, it would have been in December when the war should end and demilitarisation begin, then we would begin the serious -- these were just the stages of operative collection of intelligence. At the moment when the investigative activities would begin and when we requested for other organs to be involved, that would be the moment when the president would be informed about it, that is to say, the end. That was about a month, that was according to my plan, it should have been the month of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you had that secret operative investigation and got the result, you did not want to report that to Mr. Karadzic? You said that last week. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, there are stages when all services and all police services in the world work secretly on collection of information, and there is a stage when they report other levels. The president of the republic is not an issue of Radovan Karadzic but the institution of the president of the republic. Once the information is collected and verified and you reach the point when there are grounds to suspect that certain groups of people committed such crimes, then reporting comes into play. But my manner of reporting throughout the war, from 1992 and onwards, towards the president, the reporting system was not to say something, nor did Karadzic accept this, nor did I have such a relation with him that we would speak tete-a-tete, something that would be discussed only between Tomo Kovac and Radovan Karadzic. No. I should have the evidence and the information and be ready for a new situation that would arise. I knew quite well, considering the situation, the state of minds among the soldiers on the front lines. There was a moment when we would have to begin this catharsis, when we would have to inform everyone and take measures. That could only be done after the end of the war, not at all during the war, because considering the situation that we had at the time, a civil war would have broke out amongst us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now show to the witness 1D71120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From January 1994, in which you request additional information in order to be able to report to the Presidency. Do explain to us a little bit. You told us recently that throughout the war you waited to have complete information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 1D71120, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it so we don't ... "Reports were submitted only by the CSB Sarajevo and Banja Luka, so we are not in the situation to report to the highest government leaders. "The CSB that did not submit are obliged to submit the reports no later than the 19th of January, 1994, at 10.00 a.m.," then you list which CSBs you mean, "and Sarajevo, they only submitted statistical data and not a description of important events, which is also their obligation." How does this document fit into what you just said, that throughout the war you could only report when you had complete information?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear that the Ministry of the Interior, for all information that it would forward to the government and especially the president of republic in war time, would have to have them under certain categories, for the simple reason that it would be clearly separated what sort of events they are. Was it the commission of crimes or war operations? If it's crimes, what category of crimes? This is part of the methodology of our work and it's our legal obligation. It's also the methodology that we were applying at the time so as not to mix up the qualifications once such reports reach the presidents and the governments so that they wouldn't have to try and clear it up and interpret the law. So in the items in the reports, these issues have to be identified and legally defined and clearly treated. So that's the substance here when we criticise certain centres and organs and call upon them to provide top-quality information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And a bit lower down, just before the last paragraph you say: "You should provide answers only for crimes for which criminal reports were filed or which were committed in a specific time-period, the time, that is to say, the year, when a specific crime was committed." So only for what was reported as a criminal report, not just rumours?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, essentially the ministry can only register and report about something that has been qualified as a crime or criminal events. That's the specific role of the ministry. Whether these are misdemeanours or whatever it is, it has to be qualified as such, so it cannot be arbitrary. Notes from diaries, what someone may think about something and so on, this is what I don't agree with. Any kinds of diaries, journals, something that is discovered and later assessments, there are no later assessments, just the registration and qualification of phenomena and situations. That was the assessment that was requested from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we can also show who signed this document. What's its provenance? Can we please scroll down so as to show the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's one of my memos, yes, Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives number MFI D3976, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last question, just something about language issues, which are great issues for us. I'm not going to go into the passive form. They had to report and so on, something else. The Prosecution asked you how it was possible that someone of your subordinates would be sent to a meeting and that someone like that was present at a meeting, met someone and did not report that to you. Can you please tell the Chamber, do you make a difference, a distinction, between a meeting and then encounter, and what was it that your subordinate had to inform you about and what he didn't have to inform you about?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To distinguish the military terms and military relations vis-à-vis the Ministry of the Interior, here specifically Dragomir Vasic is whom I had in mind. He was the chief of the Zvornik security centre. Certain legal issues from the purview of public security, such as securing persons and facilities in the area, are not carried out on the basis of orders. It's his original legal duty, so he's obliged to act in accordance with the law at any given moment. Depending on the situation, he has to react properly. On the other hand, it's also his right in his own territory to take part in all agreements and discussions that have to do with security and safety of civilians, whether civilians have to be transported or secured in a certain area. It's his original legal obligation. He doesn't need an order of Tomo Kovac or the minister or anyone else. It's his obligation to be involved. The manner in which he needs to report -- he doesn't need to report to me. He has to make lawful and legal agreements and go through procedures at the lower level, the police stations, their obligations which again have to be in accordance with their original legal obligations. The competences and relations of the work of the police and the way the army is commanded and controlled are mixed up here all the time. The army has strict rules; their duties are quite different. They have direct reporting and direct orders. However, the Ministry of the Interior is an organ of administration, an organ which directly implements the laws, directly provides qualifications, acts in a preventive manner, pre-emptively, it provides guide-lines, and has a repressive element also when it needs to secure and take other lawful measures, all other lawful measures. It was clear here, I never had the need to issue a document for Vasic, and as far as I know, you also did not appoint him by any act as someone who would be involved in the Srebrenica activities in connection with securing the movement of civilians and so on. But it was his legal obligation to show up there, to have information, and to be able to guide and direct the police along the whole axis and also to monitor the civilians and their movement in terms of their security and everything else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Mr. Kovac, I think you were speaking too fast for the interpreters to catch up. Before I ask you to repeat your answer. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the question. He's going into a defence of Vasic's actions along the road and what Vasic 's duties were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with that. Yes, I'll leave it to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this: If he encounters someone and it's not a meeting which is beyond his competences, does he have to ask you about this encounter or report to you about it? If it's just an encounter. I'm talking about your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to express this again, precisely because of the gentleman from the OTP, because they do not understand this part regarding the police. It's his legal obligation and he's also entitled to participate in meetings that come under the purview of his activities, but it's not envisaged at all that he has to have some contact with the minister. Imagine if so many policemen, who were directly doing things, requested powers and authorisation from the minister of the interior to do anything. It's their obligation to act and work in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I have one question about the secret operative investigation you conducted in sometime late September 1995. Do you remember you said that? Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was it like? What did you do in concrete terms and how did you conduct that investigation? You appointed somebody, in concrete terms, and he did what? I hope you understood my question.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly because I directly participated. In view of the complexity and the possibility of having people's lives threatened, the people who were working on this, so this was done secretly, I mean with exactly four tasks that were supposed to be dealt with. So whether there were any forces of Serbia in the Srebrenica operation, whether any of their forces participated in the commission of the crimes, who issued the order to attack Srebrenica, and who issued the order to execute the prisoners. Nothing else, not further in depth, not further in breadth, just these four questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll deal with it one by one. You talked about four tasks. At the end you said: Who issued the order to execute the prisoners. So before -- in order to reach that, you have to establish there's -- there was a massacre at the -- does it mean that you already knew at that time there was a massacre, execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, at the request, that is to say, at the request of our colleagues, the man who was preparing Dayton, we got these clear questions. So that means that we got these clear questions that I've already mentioned. I got them from the man who took part in preparing Dayton, in the preparations for Dayton. That was the end of September/October, so it was just before Dayton. That was the last part before the Dayton Agreement. So these were the questions. Also there can be this question whether Stanisic had already known that -- I mean certain -- well, that certain crimes had been committed, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we now have the four tasks you were asked about, and then you told us that it was done very secretly and it was very dangerous. Please tell us in more detail what you did. How did you conduct your investigation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, through talks with people who held the highest positions in the service of the military security -- well, not to go further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, please tell us in concrete terms. You asked some -- whose -- somebody to have a word with somebody in the military. Could you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I mean, among other things, I directly spoke to these people from the military, but I would not say now who they were. I can tell you what kind of things I learned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. No. If necessary, we may go into private session to protect the privacy or identity of the person who talked to you, but I'd like to know the real names who you talked to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we talked to about that situation; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who did you talk to, to know the situation, in the military? You said you investigated, probably you need some -- you must have needed an interview or talk, whatever, in whatever form. So who did you talk to at the time when you conducted that secret operative investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- if you wish to have closed session, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the best thing would be to move into closed session then, and then we will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see no problem. We'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I see the time. We'll try to finish in five minutes. Yes, could you repeat what you said about Mr. Mladic's state at the time, in brief terms.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the statement was, with regard to the mentioned persons, that from the death of his daughter onwards, Mladic was in a state that seemed schizophrenic at certain moments. He was a man who had these mood swings and his capacity was diminished then in his attitude towards events and people. Ljubomir Beara knew that and how, and he very skillfully manipulated in these events, manipulated Mladic. And at the moment of one of these states of his and when he was not at certain places, then he gave statements that Mladic had ordered him -- I mean, this is a reference to executions. He manipulated quickly and issued orders on Mladic's behalf, although I did not find any concrete direct orders issued by Mladic to him. So this entire process of organisation and speed -- because all of this happened within the course of a day. I must say that I was surprised at the speed. The bus left -- I mean, it's not that I knew it at the moment, but I investigated this later on. The buses went in one direction towards the barracks and then they were redirected to another direction and they came to a place where the pits had already been dug. I must say that I was surprised. I was surprised as far as that is concerned. But the co-ordination of Beara, I mean parallel co-ordination of preparation and execution, this decision was made during the day and he co-ordinated the commission of that crime. Beara was a man who had very strong authority from the previous -- from the previous position he held, everything that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I come to my final question. Upon the request of Jovica Stanisic from -- in Serbia, you initiated a secret operative investigation and you talked to certain individuals and you found out what happened. So this is my question: So as a -- if you could establish what happened in the capacity of minister of interior MUP, Mr. Karadzic, on the part of Mr. Karadzic, it must have been much easier for him to find out what happened? If minister could have found out what happened, Karadzic -- Mr. President should have done it much easier. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The president cannot do without us. The president cannot do without us, the organs of investigation. We are his eyes and ears. He cannot find out without us knowing. Without the organs of the military security and the civilian security, he cannot find out. The ones from the military security, of course they were the perpetrators and they closed the circle. We from the Ministry of the Interior were not in charge. We moved slowly with the gathering of information, and if you analyse everything I did during the war, I certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- would have completed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- he could have asked you to find out what happened?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that he could have asked. It was my duty to do that and -- well, you know, not to report to him -- there are these references to reporting here all the time. The most important things, revealing, discovering the causes, the facts, everything, everything that has to do with what happened, full discovery of what had happened, that was my aim, and he certainly would have received all of that from me, in a serious form and already prepared. I mean, the organ of the police, the -- would have been prepared to react to that newly created situation. I knew specifically during the war what it meant when such things are put on the table before the state organs, what one had to be prepared for. Again, I repeat that demilitarisation was very important for us. And you keep mentioning Stanisic. Maybe I should explain this to you, the preparation of Dayton. Stanisic was the man who was in charge of preparing Dayton. I worked with Stanisic for international institutions for releasing the members of UNPROFOR. On the other hand, people already knew that it wasn't Karadzic that was going to Dayton but that Milosevic was going, heading the delegation. So Milosevic headed the Serb delegation for the preparation of Dayton, so certainly he needed information. At that moment, the problem of Srebrenica cropped up. Now, whether there was an organised criminal enterprise, where the order came from, who the perpetrators were, how grave this was, and to what extent was all of Serbia involved, that is to say, the country, the government, that is why that was very important. I went into this investigation, to find out, to clarify, who the exact perpetrators were, not to have the entire Serbian people charged with this. So that was one of the requests put forth to me for this operative investigation, and no one could have done that at the time except for me or have contact with these persons except -- I mean, the persons I mentioned a moment ago. And to have that kind of relationship so that these persons could and would talk to me that way. I think that the situation is clear to you now with regard to this entire event and this entire investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I -- would dare, [Interpretation] would dare talk, that is not reflected in the transcript, would dare talk to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I think that concludes your evidence, Mr. Kovac. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, but we'll rise all together. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 20 past. I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dmicic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A reminder to both of us, we should make a short pause between questions and answers so that everything is recorded properly. Could you tell us, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have given a statement and, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D09360.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you, is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just make a longer pause, please. Have you read the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I've read and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there anything that was not recorded correctly that you would like to change?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9, it has to do with the terminology and the word "killing." Here it says "killings," and we were actually talking about two murders. We were talking about the events in Srebrenica. So, if possible, I should like these two words to be replaced by the word "events."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe the problem is in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English I can't see it. I will read to you the English version so that our official interpreters interpret it. [In English] "I recall two of my meetings with President Karadzic during the period of July 1995, as reflected in President Karadzic's appointment book. On 10th of July, together with General Subotic, between 13.45 and 14.20, and on 17th of July, between 8.30 and 8.55 [sic], when I spoke with him privately."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we received -- could we look at -- in the English version it's missing and in the Serbian version "killings" are mentioned. We should see another version, 1D49000. That's the signed Serbian version. [In English] English should say the same, but ... [Interpretation] Could we take a look at the last page to see if this is the signed version and then we'll come back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This version is different from what you -- we saw earlier on; correct? So this is the most recent one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously the old version containing errors had been uploaded and this is the latest version. We just need to see the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just wondering whether I have an old version. Very well. It -- let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 2 now to see paragraph 9 and how it reads in this signed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this version, too, the Serbian version differs from the English one. What would you like to change here in paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: The topic of discussion were the events or the developments in Srebrenica. The rest of the text is consistent with this word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now dictate this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just -- I'm not sure. Mr. Karadzic, could you ask -- deal with this matter with the witness live. I don't know what he is talking about. So could you lead live in -- with respect to this part later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from this paragraph, Professor Dmicic, does the statement faithfully reflect what you have stated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you now the same questions, would your answers be the same as in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: My answers would be identical to the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this statement be admitted with the exception of paragraph 9 which we will deal with live?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But paragraph 9 is related to the -- all paragraphs following it. So I would like you to deal with the witness live what was discussed at those two meetings. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So what is admitted as the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness first before you introduce the remainder of his testimony in the form of summary? Why don't you just start asking the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we remove this statement from the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us how many meetings we had in July 1995 and what we discussed? First of all, explain how these meetings were possible? Where were your headquarters and how often did we meet, on what occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: As head of your office, chef de cabinet - and I noted in my statement that the office consisted of two parts, the civilian and the military one - my encounters with the president took place as required by me or by him in my capacity as chief of office. My meetings with the president related to affairs which were in the purview of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when we met around mid-June 1995, what was the reason for these meetings and what was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Two meetings took place on the 10th and on the 17th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Mr. Karadzic asked about meetings in mid-June. Is it mid-July?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: July, July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please continue, Mr. Dmicic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Pronunciation in our language, "Jun," "Jul," is very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Both times the issues had to do with activities regarding reports about events in Srebrenica and the preparation or, more precisely, my participation in the legal and technical drafting of documents that needed to be drafted at the president's office during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At those meetings, did we have at our disposal any information about crimes and did we discuss crimes, the two of us, or anyone else in our presence?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: At that time, we did not have in our possession any written reports about the events in Srebrenica, nor did we discuss issues that revolved around the military events in Srebrenica. I must emphasise that I headed the civilian part of the office, and my purview had to do only with civilian affairs, that is, the functioning of the executive authorities, the judiciary, and the legislative powers as opposed to the military part of the cabinet. The military side of events happened in line with what the president always insisted on. He wanted a strict observance of the law and the rule of law and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you come to serve in my office? What were the requirements for that job? Why did we invite you for an interview? What was your previous experience?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Before joining the office of President Karadzic, I spent almost ten years doing various jobs at the Presidency of the then-Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I served as advisor, chief of office of the then-president, deputy general-secretary, and for a while I was acting general-secretary. At that time, I followed closely the developments in our political life.
