I was very familiar with the personality and the work of the president as an intellectual, a literary man, a physician, a very committed man in those difficult times for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I held in special esteem everything that in his work spoke to his commitment, his fairness, his commitment to justice and law, his communicative and constructive approach, his visionary approach to the solution of the Bosnia-Herzegovina crisis. I'll mention just a few events from those years. We were on a quest for a new legal and constitutional model for Bosnia-Herzegovina because it was already clear that the Yugoslav Federation was going to break up. He maintained a very constructive dialogue with members and representatives of other republics and parties. A quest was going on for a solution to the issue of referendum because the referendum was the trigger for the tragedies that occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And finally, he was in dialogue with representatives of international organisations and institutions. Simply, he had a passion for the truth, a passion for the search for solutions, with a very strong awareness that an error in a serious matter could sometimes be worse than a crime. His openness and his multi-lateral view of all issues led to high-quality solutions, and what I felt at the time, as a lawyer and an activist with long experience and a long-serving employee of the state authorities and state agencies, gave me a guarantee that his was the right road for preserving the identity and the autochthonous nature of not only the Serbian but all the other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And taking a synthetic view, a solution that would enable Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain a part of Yugoslavia, while allowing the Serb people and all the others who accepted the Serb people to live together in Republika Srpska or, alternatively, that the Serbian people take a separate way out. Those were the challenges that we were facing at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can fairly stop here. The question was how come you served Mr. Karadzic? For saving time, could we go back to the statement? Can we upload them, both versions, in B/C/S and in English? Para 9. We want to check the veracity of English translation in this statement. So could you kindly read out slowly paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "As for the killings of people from Srebrenica, I can confirm that I remember two of my meetings with President Karadzic from this period. The killings of people in Srebrenica, namely: On the 10th of July, 1995, together with General Subotic from 13.45 hours until 14.20 hours, as well as on the 17th of July, 1995, from 18.30 hours until 18.55 hours, when I talked to him privately."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, with the witness's explanation about the correction and the evidence led live so far, we can safely admit his statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter? Do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection with respect to any associated exhibits? One item, 1D9362, which was referred to in paragraph 9 -- 18, does not form an inseparable and indispensable part in the view of the Chamber. Do you have any objection to the remaining two?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll receive the statement as well as two associated exhibits. Shall we assign the numbers now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D49000 get the Exhibit Number D3977; the 65 ter number 1D09360 receives the Exhibit Number D3978; and the 65 ter number 1D09362 receives the Exhibit Number D3979. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said 1D9362 will not be admitted, so what we are admitting is 61 and 63. So that will be corrected accordingly. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, just to complete this answer to a limited question, does that mean that you were a chef de cabinet and the general-secretary and the deputy of the general-secretary in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina even before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. I had been that for several years, between 1984 up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the elections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- did the SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can first introduce the summary of his evidence for the benefit of the public, because we admitted his statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I will now read the statement, or rather, the summary of Professor Dmicic's statement. I will read it in English. [In English] Mile Dmicic served as chef de cabinet to the president of Republika Srpska from the end of 1993 until after the Dayton Agreement. He also served as the secretary-general to the president of the Republika Srpska from 1994. He is presently a constitutional law professor at the University of Banja Luka. During July 1995 he was working in President Karadzic's cabinet. He recalls that on 10th of July, 1995, he met President Karadzic together with General Subotic. During this meeting, President Karadzic informed them that the combat operations around Srebrenica continued with a view to completely demilitarising Srebrenica and ordered them to prepare a decision proclaiming a state of war in the municipality of Srebrenica-Skelani, which they did. He had another meeting with President Karadzic on 17th of July, 1995. During this meeting, they discussed a declaration signed by Miroslav Deronjic and the representative of the Muslim civilian authorities of the Srebrenica that indicated that the evacuation of the population had been carried out properly. Professor Dmicic also saw President Karadzic on numerous other times during July 1995 and could see him without having an appointment. He never heard any discussion about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica in July 1995. He never heard President Karadzic saying anything that would indicate that he was informed about the execution of prisoners. He never saw anything in any document received by the president in July 1995 that would point to the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica. Mr. Dmicic worked closely with President Karadzic for more than two years. He knows that President Karadzic would never have been in favour of executing prisoners under any circumstances. He regarded President Karadzic as a very humane person and someone who cared for people of all religious beliefs and ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I can, I would just like to complete by asking whether after the multi-party elections the SDS requested that someone else be in your position or was it requested from you to become a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you selected your associates, including myself, in accordance with the principle of quality and experience - that was your choice - also loyalty to general interest, I would say. You never requested me, even though someone may have exerted pressure on you, to become a member of either the Serbian Democratic Party or to sign any sort of special personal declarations. That by itself confirms that the attitude, to you, and the general interest was based on a belief which I shared with you as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dmicic, as you have noted, the most part of your evidence was admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dmicic, I want to clarify another position which you held prior to serving as head of office for Dr. Karadzic. You were appointed to the SDS regionalisation staff in September 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Just, if I may provide a short commentary. This organisational, or rather, actional form was tasked with gaining certain insights into the organisation and life, the social standing, certain processes, not only among the Serbian population but in those parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the local communities, in which the Serbian population was predominant. Considering that for several previous years before the period that you are talking about, some negative processes had begun in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the issue was to contribute to a good, high-quality, and legalistic resolution of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina because those forms of the local organisation of population were not established by the constitution. It was a pro-active approach, care for the people and the law, regardless of the political, religious, or any other affiliations. It was all done in a completely peaceful atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Fine. We'll just deal with this quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25531, please. Can we go to page 2, please, in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just so we're all clear, this is the decision on the appointment of the regionalisation staff, and I'll just read under the heading 1: "The Staff for monitoring the implementation of the Decision on the proclamation of autonomous regions as inseparable parts of the federal state of federative Yugoslavia and constituent parts of the federal unit of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as on the removal of populated places from one municipality and their inclusion in the formation of another municipality, is hereby appointed ..." And then you're listed as one of the members; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: -- true that I was a member, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we admit that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what, Mr. Dmicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that this was just a form of response or reaction to the processes that had been initiated by teams coming from the other two ethnicities. All the members of these boards were employees of the republican organs, that is to say, the state administration organs, government organs. None of them went out into the field, none of them directly met, none of them produced any documents, none of them established any organisational or other forms. This actually lasted but briefly. As far as I remember, it was very brief. This is actually a reflection of the processes which had been going on since the beginning of the 1990s in the Yugoslav Federation, and then also a reflection of the processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One really needs to be well-versed in the history of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me just say this: Not in the last 500 years since the disappearance of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina which existed in the Middle Ages, these three ethnicities did not have the same position, either historically or ethnically or regionally or culturally. They did not have unity in any of these aspects, a unity on which they could firmly rely in order to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1990s. So therefore, our -- we strove towards preserving Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the primary task, to preserve it and to have it remain in the Yugoslav state. And in the Yugoslav state there were two --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's -- that's enough, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: -- ethnicities that were dominant, the Serbs and the Bosniaks, judging by the figures from that period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be brief in answering questions as much as possible in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could I have that document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives Exhibit Number P6484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll go to July 1995, please. Now you refer in your statement to a statement signed on the 17th of July by Deronjic, Nesib Mandzic and Franken, an UNPROFOR representative. You're aware, aren't you, that a supposed agreement articulated in this statement wasn't genuine, was it? It in no way reflected, did it, the reality, the reality for the Muslim civilian population in Potocari, which had no alternative but to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I don't know about this nor did I have any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, this is what the UNPROFOR representative who signed the statement, Franken, this is what he said about it. I'm just going to read it rather than ask for it to be shown. He said this: "The part of the document stating that the population can remain in the enclave or evacuate is nonsense because they did not have a realistic opportunity to stay or to move in any direction. These people didn't have a choice. Staying in a small area with no means to survive controlled by the Serbs, being afraid and lethargic as they were, that is not a choice. It was ordered that they should go to the Kladanj area. It was not a decision by the representatives but an order of Mladic to go to the area of Kladanj." That's in his statement, P04175, at paragraph 105. Now, this declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just clarify with the witness whether this was written in the document, did Franken write this in the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Karadzic, do not intervene in such a way. Ms. Pack made it clear that this is part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This declaration signed on the 17th of July was created to disseminate the lie that the Muslim population had left the enclave voluntarily, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: That's what you say. I as a lawyer believe a signed and a certified document to be a public document. So anyone, including myself who had the occasion to see the document, I couldn't doubt its validity. The statements given after the signing and the announcement, public announcement of this document, can be the subject of a different sort of inspection but not of -- a subject of a question directed at me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You agree, don't you, Mr. Dmicic, that the civilian population in Potocari had no alternative but to leave, they had no food, no shelter, they were scared. You agree that that was the reality, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question because I had no information about that aspect of life in Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I dealt with completely different issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No information? You are aware that by the 17th of July international news media were reporting, weren't they, that thousands of terrified people had been deported from Srebrenica and that men of fighting age had been taken away for screening by 17th July; you're aware of those reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Everyone who was watching or listening to the media could notice that that was not just reporting an information, but in terms of the Serbian people in Republika Srpska it was propaganda. And I suppose, though I cannot claim, I did not do any research about this, the propaganda has quite a different purpose. It was difficult for everyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, life was not so stark, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not talking about supposed Muslim propaganda; I'm talking about international news reporting. You're aware of press reports in the British newspaper, "The Independent," by a journalist called Robert Block, on the 14th through the 17th of July and a number of days thereafter, you're aware of that reporting?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of these reports, but looking at the wider picture we could not hear good news or, to be more specific, objective, truthful, and proper information that would relate to the people I belonged to, practically throughout the tragic conflict that existed in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Robert Block wrote a report on the 14th of July, just prior -- in the days prior to this declaration that you've referred to in your statement, and I'll quote what he says. It's P04396. He says: "International resolve over Bosnia came under renewed pressure yesterday with reports of new atrocities against Muslim refugees as the Bosnian Serbs deported thousands of terrified people from the Srebrenica enclave in the biggest ethnic cleansing operation of the war," he wrote. And then he said later: "Men of fighting age had been taken away by the Bosnian Serbs for what they said was screening." This is on the 14th of July. You didn't hear any of these sorts of reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear. Part of the cabinet staff was also an advisor for public relations or relations with the media. I did not hear about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, let's look at your role as head of office and secretary-general. You told us this morning that you were concerned with civilian as opposed to military affairs. Your role as head of office included, did it, organising meetings for the president, receiving visitors, reviewing the mail, preparing responses to mail; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it had to do with issues from the civilian life of Republika Srpska, and I was primarily focused on the constitutional organs of Republika Srpska. But just for a moment I will go back to supplement what I said in one of my previous answers. The enclave and the demilitarisation of Srebrenica was supposed to be carried out in two days. The enclave had existed for practically two years and several months. It was the obligation of the international community to carry out the demilitarisation. In view of the duties that I was charged with, there was no need for me to remember and I cannot remember the wider context that you are directing my attention to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you've told us your responsibilities, civilian affairs as opposed to Subotic's area, which was military affairs, and you've agreed with me, haven't you, that you opened mail, reviewed mail, prepared responses for the president; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that is mail within the life of the republic, within the civilian activity of the organs and institutions of Republika Srpska, not the military mail. If you meant reports, that was not within my purview, within the duties I had on the basis of instructions issued by the president of the republic. I repeat once again, the office also had advisors for certain activities and I confirm that for the activities that you have just asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, well, I want to ask you about mail, not military mail. You would have been aware, wouldn't you, of the letter sent to Dr. Karadzic by Mazowiecki, the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights, on the 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And can we have it up? It's P06396.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not know about that. That question can be addressed directly to the advisor for international relations, for public opinion and so on, and you already had an opportunity of speaking to him in this very place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could we have page 3, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, you were head of the office, right, so you would have opened mail, reviewed it, when it came into the office?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that in peace time it would look that way. We worked 24 hours, people say even more than 24 hours. For almost three years I could not be on duty and awake for 24 hours a day. Nature did not bestow that gift upon me, so I have nothing to say in relation to that letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You haven't had a chance to look at it yet. Perhaps familiarise yourself with it and see if you remember it. 24th of July, 1995. It's in English, I'm afraid. Can you understand English?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read it to you if you're unable to read it. It says: "Dear Sir, "I would like to express my deepest concern regarding the recent events in the Srebrenica area which resulted in the forced displacement of some 40.000 individuals. It has been reported that as a result of these events, several thousand individuals are unaccounted for, and there is fear that many of these have other been killed or detained." And then it goes on in the last paragraph: "I would therefore appreciate your co-operation in allowing the field staff of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights to assess the human rights situation ..." et cetera. And then it says: "... in particular by granting access to those who have been detained during the recent events." Signed by the special rapporteur. You were aware, weren't you, of July 1995, 24th July 1995, of this letter, this letter to Dr. Karadzic stating that thousands had been forcibly displaced, several thousand or unaccounted for, feared dead?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Looking at the text of the letter, I can just conclude that this letter was addressed personally to the president of the republic. Letters addressed this way on envelopes went to the president of the republic directly, perhaps not all of them, depending on the situation. As I've already said, that was not peace time. Life was a lot more dynamic, a lot more difficult, and a lot more tempestuous than is normally the case. I really cannot remember even the appearance, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So your evidence is then that this wouldn't have gone through you to the president; it would have gone directly to him?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I can just make an assumption, but I cannot give an answer to that who gave this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't deny, do you, the truth of the international reports, reporting as early as July 1995 that mass executions of Muslim men took place after the fall of Srebrenica? You don't deny the truth of those reports, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I would like you to tell me even more specifically what your question directed to me actually is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't deny, sitting here today, do you, Mr. Dmicic, that many thousands of Muslim men were executed following the fall of Srebrenica by Bosnian Serb armed forces? You don't deny that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. At that time I had no knowledge about that, especially at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Gordan Milinic and other of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The question was: Sitting here today whether you know or not. You said at that time you had no knowledge. And now do you deny that many thousands of Muslims were executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even today I don't have any knowledge about that, that I would - as a valid document - take into account as my conviction in terms of what had happened at the time. Independently who -- even if this is the rapporteur of the United Nations, everyone submits reports to those who had actually given instructions to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking about then. I'm now asking you about now, today, and whether today you accept the truth of the matter, the truth that thousands of Muslim men were executed following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge and I cannot accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have a lot of trouble hearing the witness. Could he please be asked to come closer to the microphone and could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dmicic, could you come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Another of Dr. Karadzic's advisors testified here a few months ago and said that the Srebrenica graveyard was a farce, the whole thing was a set-up. Is that your position too?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: To a considerable part, yes. Certainly it is hard to speak about the tragedy of that area at the time with feelings, especially the history of memory in the Balkans is very tragic and dismal. In recent history, likewise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to ask --

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one is investigating or recording who is being buried in those areas or some other areas. It is hard to have insight into that, but of course, we have compassion for the tragedy of each and every individual, not only members of a particular ethnic or religious group in Bosnia-Herzegovina or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to ask about one more document, and that is P02288. It's a letter from Mr. Akashi to Dr. Karadzic, dated the 14th of August, 1995. And it's the second page in English and the third page in B/C/S. There's a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you put that question. A minute ago you said, when asked about the execution of Muslim men, you said you didn't have any knowledge. "I don't have any knowledge and I cannot accept that." And then you said you felt compassion and then you said about tragedy. Not knowing what happened, how can you say it was a tragedy? Can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I need to clarify myself, it would be sufficient to see anyone's grave or any graveyard in Bosnia-Herzegovina that came into being during these tragic conflicts and to have, therefore, an identical attitude like the one I referred to in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking for graveyards, you're aware of this letter to Karadzic dated the 12th of August, 1995. First paragraph I'm referring to where it says this -- refers to the UN Security Council Resolution of the 10th of August, 1995, and it says: Deep concern, and I'm paraphrasing, at the fact that many of the former inhabitants of Srebrenica are not accounted for, "I'm equally concerned at these reports, especially at the allegation of the existence of a mass grave identified by the Government of the United States ..." This is a letter which would have come across your desk of which you would have been aware, you would have been aware of its contents, right, August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: No. Such letters were never on my desk. There was an advisor for this field. An expression of deep concern is the initial sentence in most of the communications coming from the international community. Mass graves in such a small area like the enclave of Srebrenica would cover practically the entire urban area or the area of the enclave. You should take into account the size of the enclave in these conditions; that is to say, mass graves could only be -- experiencing all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska where graves and graveyards are scattered about but of members of all the ethnic communities. I have no information about the letter that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you're well aware, aren't you, that the Republika Srpska government wrote its own report, set up a commission which carried out its own investigation into the events in Srebrenica in 2004 which concluded, didn't it, that between the 10th and 19th July 1995, several thousands of Bosniaks were liquidated and that the perpetrators among the others -- among others undertook measures to cover-up the crime by relocating the bodies. I'm paraphrasing a bit, but that's what it concluded. You know about that report, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the reference for that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. P06220. It's not notified but I hadn't planned to bring it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're aware of those conclusions, aren't you, RS commission?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I know about the work of that commission from the media. I did not have an opportunity, and in 2004 I was not in that position to have that document be made available to me. I cannot speak about a positive or a negative attitude, particularly not to say anything about the number of victims. But, however, you have to follow in continuity what happened in the discussions about that report after 2004. I am not going to assert anything, but I'm going to present my point of view. The truth about the validity of this document cannot be considered a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I've no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very few, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, can we start with the most recent matter, this document, the discussions that took place later. Can you tell us whether this report is uncontested and in which conditions the government signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: We are talking about knowledge coming from the media. In the public opinion it is believed that this was done under pressure. That is why I'm saying, though not claiming full capacity for my statement, that this is still a document that, if I could say, from a procedural point of view, is yet to be proven. We have read a great many facts, heard many facts, and commented upon many facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of pressure is this under which this report was made?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: The pressure was identified in the public as having come from some international organisations and associations, but, I repeat, this number has not -- is not something that I heard from any source in any structure in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government included. In actual fact, it would be less than the number referred to in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These pressures at the time -- well, what kind of danger were those who admitted this document exposed to? Were there any sanctions at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Precisely in the spirit of what you said, threats of the then-president of the republic and further on. In the public it was believed that a certain report had to be arrived at. I don't have much information about that, but I accept your assessment as earmarking the situation concerning that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the president of the republic. Was any president of the republic dismissed in some way?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's a leading question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One was on the 7th of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: These are leading questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leading and -- he's just saying he heard from the public. I'm not sure whether it has any probative value at all. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, on page 68, Akashi's letter was shown, the letter he sent me, and you said that it had not been on your desk. Can you remember where you were and where I was at the time when this letter arrived? Do you have any recollection of that? So from the 10th of August onwards.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but my absence could have taken place in Banja Luka only. That is to say, although I first spoke about myself, I can assume that that was the time of this joint stay in Banja Luka and in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P4424 -- or 42, and then the 8th of August, that entry. I'll tell you in a handwritten part it is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I was convinced that I said the correct number. [Interpretation] Yes, just a moment, please. Could we please have the entry for the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this means, that at Sokolac, at 2.00, gynaecology operation, technical means, you have both pages. We can move on to the 10th of August. So the 8th and 9th, Sokolac and Srbinje.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now, the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what it says for the 10th and 11th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I cannot see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see where the cursor is. Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Ah, Krajina, yes. That's the Krajina period. That is Banja Luka and that part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could we leaf through up until the 18th or 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, this empty space for the 16th and 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means your absence from the seat of the Presidency in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did we first appear at the office?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It's only a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It is the 19th, yes. The 18th is empty. It's the calendar that's empty, and then the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, on page 60-something, it was suggested to you that civilians from Srebrenica were forced to leave and Mazowiecki was quoted there. Do you know what kind of reputation Mr. Mazowiecki enjoyed among our people, to what extent he could be trusted? If you don't know, then we'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: He was not really trusted in terms of facts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at D3401. D3401.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram from Ambassador Akashi to Mr. Annan, who was then under-secretary, not yet Secretary-General. I'll read out paragraph 2 in English: [In English] "Paragraph 5 should take account of the fact that, according to UNHCR, a great majority of the residents of Srebrenica do not wish to remain there. They are already displaced persons from elsewhere and will wish to move on." [Interpretation] According to your peripheral view of these things, is this comment by Akashi more consistent with the real situation as opposed to Mazowiecki's assertion that these people had been forced out?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi's words reflect the situation more realistically, but speaking of this term, an overwhelming majority or great majority, we have to bear in mind the total population of that enclave. That number was not as large as it was presented. That's at least what I think. I cannot claim anything for certain and I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 61, you mentioned that the president had an advisor for the media, a media advisor. Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It's Mr. Jovan Zametica, who, in addition to dealing with international co-operation and relations, talks and receptions, also covered the media because he is a connoisseur of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last topic: You are a professor of constitutional law. Could you tell the Chamber, from the legal point of view, were there any constitutional possibilities for the creation of new municipalities, for moving one local commune from one municipality to another, and what was allowed or not at the time when regionalisation plans were being made by all three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not relevant to the content of P6484, regionalisation staff? I'm -- not knowing the document, I have no clue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall respond, Your Excellencies. You are right because the Prosecution suggested that Professor Dmicic had been caught-out in some party activity, otherwise why would I have put that document forth --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- those are people who worked on behalf of political parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before we continue, our Registrar has something to announce for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the transcript record, I would like to note that we were in open session at the moment when we took the break at 12.44 [sic]. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we show the redacted version of this document, 65 ter 25592.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Professor, were there any constitutional possibilities for internal reorganisation of municipalities or the formation even of associations of municipalities and the movement of local communes to whatever ethnic community they belonged?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: In the constitutional system as established in 1974, that is to say, the last Yugoslav constitution, municipalities were able to associate themselves along the lines of self-management or to form associations. The first type was voluntary and the second one was firmer. They would form associations for economic reasons and interests and to develop certain industries, et cetera. Later on, in the period when regional communities were formed, precisely that model was used because in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were 22 such regional associations of municipalities and they were established on the basis of so-called self-management agreements and socio-economic agreements based on joint interests. However, when we in the republic realised that it was not necessary because the system of operation of these communities has reached such a level of development, that system of regional organising was abolished because it was no longer necessary. Because its first purpose was to provide us mutual assistance and protection, all those things that were destroyed with the dissolution of Yugoslavia. And to repeat, that was a legitimate way of solving some common issues on smaller territories through organisation and association within the regional system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now read the part in the box in this document of 17 December 1991. [In English] "The team today visited the village of Dobretic, 4.800 Croatian inhabitants, within the Serbian-dominated municipality of Skender Vakuf. "... the President of HDZ and the president of the local community expressed the wish to leave the municipality of Skender Vakuf and join either the municipalities of Jajce or Travnik, or be an independent municipality. "The Mayor and Assembly of Skender Vakuf have no objections against this plan. "The necessary procedures will be started up in the next months." [Interpretation] Is this action, this expression of Dobretic's will to change its status legitimate and was it legitimate on the part of Skender Vakuf to give its consent?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, how does it arise from the line of cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, in my understanding, the Prosecution has tried to suggest that Professor Dmicic, who at that time served as the deputy general-secretary of our common state --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In its cross-examination, the Prosecution showed a list of experts and civil servants nominated by the SDS, suggesting that they worked on the regionalisation and they suggested that Professor was engaged in party work, and we see from the indictment that the work on the territorial reorganisation of Bosnia is held against me. This document shows that even before the war it was both allowed and widely accepted that local communes changed their affiliation to municipalities. This group of experts, although nominated by the SDS, was not necessarily a party organisation of the SDS. It consisted of people who occupied positions of authority throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. And here, Your Excellencies, I want to show that this could be done and was done in peace time without any mention of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I still don't see why the legal opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The content of the appointment decision contains the passage like removal of populated places from one municipalities and their inclusion and et cetera. We'll allow the question to -- and this is your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honours. That is precisely the case, one local commune from a Serbian municipality wants to move to another municipality and the Serbian municipality does not oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, according to all you know about our constitutional system, was this activity lawful and legitimate before the war and without any war?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Transfers of local communes from one municipality to another was completely lawful and legitimate. Under those circumstances, all that was sought were not only possibilities for the system to function, but also to better meet local interests. It was done throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is still being done today. But we have to note that decision-making about reorganisation in one municipality was up to the local population. They made these decisions, and at the level of the municipality the decision was up to the local Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for coming here to testify and thank you for your co-operation at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Toholj. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Toholj, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at this Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that would -- that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that answer -- an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that what I have just told you, Mr. Toholj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Toholj.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Well, it's just in the upload, the document to which the witness is referring is at pages 3 to 5 of e-court, that's simply my observation, this is in reference to the decree 11104.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, he hasn't referred to page numbers but -- in his statement, of course. But in e-court, the document, the decree to which he's referring appears in e-court at pages 3 to 5 of the English and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In relation to the other documents, I would object to the admission of ID 10302 and 10301 and 10300, and the reason why -- the first one is concerned, 02, it's irrelevant and there's insufficient foundation laid in the relevant paragraph, 27, of the statement, in my submission. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not spend more time here. If the Defence is minded to tender those documents, I would like Mr. Karadzic to deal with them live. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now read in English a short summary of Mr. Miroslav Toholj's statement. [In English] Miroslav Toholj was the editor of "Javnost," the weekly journal of the SDS. On July the 12th, 1991, he was elected to the Main Board and then to the Executive Board of the SDS, and in August 1990, he became vice-president of the Council for Inter-Party Co-operation at the SDS. In mid-June 1992, he was appointed director of the centre for investigating war crimes against the Serbs. In February 1993, he became minister of information in the Republika Srpska government and, in October 1996, he was elected deputy at the RS National Assembly. In 1990, after the introduction of multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the SDA party was established by the Muslim intellectuals gathered around Alija Izetbegovic; then-philosophy Professor Muhamed Filipovic; Omer Behmen; Fikret Abdic; and Adil Zulfikarpasic. Dr. Zulfikarpasic and Dr. Filipovic soon distanced themselves from the party. In the meantime, the HDZ was formed. After the first multi-party elections and the convincing victory of national parties, Islamisation of society became a constant strategic goal for the SDA. The situation in the media became disastrous, and the Serbian people suffered the greatest damage as a result of the unbalanced editorial policy --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do hesitate to interrupt when Dr. Karadzic is reading the summary, but I make the observation that the summary appears to be of the previously unredact -- the unredacted version of the statement. That's my only observation. It's -- as I was listening to it, I heard reference to some of the portions of the statement that are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Maybe we have missed to follow the redaction -- to implement it on the summary, and I appreciate this warning and I would accept any warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pack. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As a reaction to Muslim propaganda, the newspaper "Javnost" was launched and eminent Serbian intellectuals initiated the revival of the Serbian cultural and educational society. Realising the danger from the growing distance between the Serbs and the Muslims, the SDS proposed that the institution of the Chamber of People be established before the elections, so that all the crucial matters in BH would be resolved by consensus, which was rejected by the Muslims. This institution was later introduced in a certain sense by the Dayton Peace Agreement, which shows that the Serbian request was deeply justified. In July 1991, the Serbian political leadership made political contact with Dr. Zulfikarpasic for the establishment of a broad coalition. Unfortunately, the Serbian-Muslim historic agreement was soon rejected by Mr. Izetbegovic. The inter-ethnic gap was becoming deeper and deeper, and the out-voting of the Serbian deputies in the parliament and some municipalities was regular practice. In such circumstances, in late October 1991, the SDS deputies and the other Serbian deputies left the common parliament and established the Assembly of the Serbian people in BH, which nevertheless insisted on the multi-ethnic principle. The inter-ethnic split culminated on October the 14th, 1991, when the Croatian and the Muslim deputies, disregarding the will of the Serbian deputies, adopted a decision proclaiming the sovereignty of BH. In response, the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH decided to conduct a national plebiscite, at which the majority of the voters rejected the constitutional change of the republic. The very establishment of the SDS was an expression of the exciting fear -- existing fear from -- among people that what happened from -- in Second World War might happen again. Before the establishment of the VRS in May 1992, Serbian towns and villages surrounded by non-Serbian population started forming Crisis Staffs of the kind that both Croats and Muslims had been establishing prior to that. Dr. Karadzic never tried to influence Mr. Toholj's work as the editor of the "Javnost" or as the minister of information. The Republika Srpska government was taken aback by the news that Srebrenica had been freed. At that time, Miroslav Toholj was at the Vatican where, even before the completion of the military operation, everyone was already talking about the horrible crimes committed in Srebrenica. This media campaign had clearly been prepared in advance. In July 1995, Mr. Toholj had contacts with Dr. Karadzic and he did not have the impression that Dr. Karadzic was aware of any violation of the customs of war and humanitarian law happening in and around Srebrenica. And that is a short summary. I don't have questions for Mr. Toholj at that moment. I will skip to deal with documents that are excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, as you understood, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, did we give the exhibit number for the statement? Let's do that now, only the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D9756 receives Exhibit Number D3981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Pack, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, as a result of the various positions you held during the war and prior, you were closely involved with the Bosnian Serb leadership in disseminating propaganda and controlling the RS media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: It is correct that I was closely involved with part of the Bosnian Serb leadership and the leadership of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I was not involved in disseminating propaganda, but rather in informing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, let's break it down. On the 13th of September, 1990, you were appointed by Dr. Karadzic as editor-in-chief of "Javnost"; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: No. In September 1990, a group of people who were later to become members of the advisory council, the inter-party advisory council, embittered by the conduct of the state-run media or what they had been up until that point, initiated the printing of a daily newspaper which would be published in the Cyrillic script for the first time since the Second World War in Bosnia-Herzegovina and which would also reflect the Serbian positions. This group of people proposed me as the editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 15087, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is a decision of the SDS BH Main Board, and if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have the English and the B/C/S up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There isn't an English in e-court that we can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies. Let me just consult with a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps just look at page 2 of the B/C/S and you can see the signature of Dr. Karadzic and the stamp. You can confirm that? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll go back to page 1 in the B/C/S and I am expecting the English to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And perhaps while we're waiting for the translation, you've obviously got the B/C/S in front of you, so you can see and confirm that this is a decision to launch "Javnost," yes? And it's dated the 13th of September, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: I can see that, but I see that this is the decision of the Main Board and the Main Board had around 40 or 50 members, and the decision is signed by the president of the party, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: This is the decision of the Main Board and those who initiated the founding of this newspaper were sitting in the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I understand it's been uploaded now, the translation. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: There we see in the plain words of the text "decision to launch Javnost," and we see signed at the bottom and just to draw your attention to the second paragraph: "The SDS BH ... shall be the founder and publisher of Javnost," you can see that. "Funds for the publication of Javnost shall be ensured from the party's special-purpose fund, donations, marketing, and sales of the paper ..." et cetera. This is the decision by which the newspaper was launched; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because each newspaper has its founder. Here the founder of the weekly "Javnost" is the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And your bottom paragraph identified: "The editor-in-chief of Javnost shall be the writer Miroslav Toholj ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies and thank you to Dr. Karadzic. It's the following page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see the last paragraph, penultimate paragraph, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd ask for this document to be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 65 ter number 15087 is -- receives the Exhibit Number P06485. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were also appointed as president of the SDS Commission for Information and Propaganda, weren't you, on 9th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25553 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, just please let me have a look at this document. No, that's not a document that I have in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Page 2, please, in the English and can we have in the B/C/S also page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And here is the decision on the appointment of the Commission for Information and Propaganda, and you can see there under the list of names, you're on the commission and then it says: "We appoint herewith Miroslav Toholj the President of the Commission for Information and Propaganda," and then we see signed by Dukic, who is the SDS president of the Executive Board. Does that all accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, it corresponds with my statement too, not only my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you were again, weren't you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could I have that admitted, please, just that page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives Exhibit Number 6486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In 1993, as a member of the SDS Executive Committee, you were again placed in charge of information and propaganda, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: In 1992, at the beginning of the war, the work of the Serbian Democratic Party was frozen, and when it started operating again, people who had been in the Main Board and in the commissions earlier were mostly, in most cases if they had survived the first year of the war, were once again in charge of their duties so that I was once again reappointed to this commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: For information and propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: For information and propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the propaganda aims of the Bosnian Serb leadership included the dissemination of information, designed to provoke fear and hatred amongst the Bosnian Serb population of Bosnian Croats and Muslims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: No, but I would like you to show me some information that would fit into that kind of characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, one of the means by which you did this was to invoke alleged crimes, crimes committed against Serbs during World War II; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: It wasn't intended for that purpose. Simply, you would have to, if you know the history of that part of the Balkans, you would have to know that it was only around 50 years after the Second World War that some facts from that war and the perishing of some peoples during the war were brought to light. I had had two victims in my family in the Second World War and that was my own grandfather whose bones were placed in our family tomb only then. So when you characterised the information of what was happening at the time as propaganda, that was the first and last time that we buried my grandfather. And in the same year they had -- he had been killed by the Croatian Ustashas. And the same year we also buried an uncle by whom I got my name. He didn't have a grave and none of our family members were allowed to visit his grave, otherwise we would have been imprisoned by communists in one of the communist prisons. He has been short by the Partizans. So after a long period of silence which was ideologically caused, it was a period when finally some facts began to surface once again. And of course we did inform the public about events at various execution sites where such things did happen during World War II.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to show you an example of the sort of public announcement that the SDS Executive Board issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: 65 ter 15085, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see on your screen a document that is generated by the SDS Executive Board stamped similarly -- in similar manner to the document we saw previously, appointing you as president of the commission of propaganda. You can see that; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, but I don't see some of the lines, they are not legible. And another thing, I don't know who signed this, who wrote it, who issued it. It was not issued by the Commission for Information and Propaganda --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's issued by, as I said to you in introducing this document, you can see it's stamped and signed "BiH SDS Executive Board." It's the same stamp we saw in the previous document by which the commission for propaganda was appointed. Now, I'm going to read to you the first two paragraphs. You can see what they say. This is a public announcement to the Serb people. "Those who want to destroy Yugoslavia are attacking the Serb people at all points and are endangering its existence and territorial unity. "Genocidal hordes attack Serb villages and cities, Serb homes and Serb babies. They now want to win the already lost Second World War and to reduce the Serb state to its borders from 1914." This public announcement by the SDS Executive Board, this was designed, wasn't it, to communicate to the Bosnian Serb population that they were in jeopardy of genocide at the hands of Bosnian Muslims and Croats, genocidal hordes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know who wrote this document. I've never seen it or read it before, and I see that there is a stamp here. We had a spokesperson within the party who acted independently, we can put it that way, on behalf of the Executive Board, maybe it was him. This document, although it was verified, it was never made public. I mean, I do not remember that it was published in the paper that I edited as the editor-in-chief. Secondly, the Serb people didn't have to be reminded in this way, or rather, no suggestions had to be made to them in terms of generating fear because the fear was already there among the people. This could have been taken as a sign that the party that was an expression of the will of the Serb people also understood that full well, that fear, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: But it is this document, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, Mr. Toholj, it's invoking the crimes of World War II as a means of engendering fear and hatred of the Muslim and Croat population in the present; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Well, I cannot accept that, that thesis of yours, never. Because the Second World War was still very vivid in the memories of the families. I've already said that somewhere. In Bosnia-Herzegovina it so happened that in the same families there were the same victims like the Second World War and this war, the perpetrators were the same, executioners as we put it in Serbian. So you cannot remove this major historical event as the Second World War was from the consciousness of the people. That would have been a miracle had someone succeeded in doing that. Even the First World War when, again, some unfortunate things happened in Sarajevo, after the assassination of Sarajevo and so on. So these are very important historical events that cannot be forgotten within a single generation. The next generation cannot be in a position not to have any awareness of that and, therefore, not fear. And especially when things happen when -- that remind them of the Second World War. You know when the chequer-board flag was chosen as the official flag of Croatia, the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were indeed reminded of the crimes that were committed in the days of the quisling Independent State of Croatia, and the crimes that were committed then were abominable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, even if it's as you say, the crimes of the Second World War were very vivid still in the memories of families, you understand, don't you, Mr. Toholj, you understood at the time, how powerful, how powerful the invocation of those crimes in documentation such as this, in announcements such as this, how powerful an effect -- what a powerful effect that implication had in generating fear and hatred in the civilian population, the Serbian population, of the Bosnian Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TOHOLJ
utterances.text: Madam, I have to ask you why and on the basis of what you are ascribing this to me personally or some influence of mine over the person or people who wrote this. This is not my language. I never intoned any of my writings with this type of vocabulary and in this way, and I really do not see how you link this up with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to admit that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't have any objection to the admission, although the witness didn't identify it, but I think it's relevant to -- for the Chamber to have it so that it can understand the context of some of the comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document number 15085 receives the Exhibit Number P6487, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Toholj, we'll adjourn for today and we'll continue tomorrow morning. I will advise you not to talk with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
